    19	\section{At a glance}
    20	
    21	\begin{itemize}
    22	  \item \textbf{Difficulty.} Medium.  The extraction proof contains two
    23	  incorrect numerical steps and later suppresses the range projection when
    24	  passing from unitary conjugation to isometry conjugation.
    25	  \item \textbf{Estimated weight.} A corrected positive-contraction estimate,
    26	  a small-error case split for normalization, and one range-projection transfer
    27	  lemma for a projective measurement family.
    28	  \item \textbf{Mathlib/project split.} Positivity, contraction inequalities,
    29	  isometry range projections, and norm estimates belong to finite-dimensional
    30	  Hilbert-space algebra.  The state-dependent family distance and register
    31	  placements are project-local.
    32	  \item \textbf{Key mathematical inputs.} The inequality
    33	  $H^2\geq2H-I$ for a positive contraction, the triangle inequality, and
    34	  $Q=\phi\phi^\dagger$ for an isometry.  The repair is tracked in
    35	  \ghissue{19}.
    36	\end{itemize}
    37	
    38	\section{Key theorem forms}
    39	
    40	Let $H_X$ and $H_Z$ be the positive contractions of the extraction proof, and
    41	let $\vartheta$ be a unit vector such that
    42	\[
    43	  \langle\vartheta,H_W\vartheta\rangle\geq1-\delta/2
    44	  \qquad (W\in\{X,Z\}).
    45	\]
    46	Since $(I-H_W)^2\geq0$,
    47	\[
    48	  H_W^2\geq2H_W-I,
    49	  \qquad
    50	  \langle\vartheta,H_W^2\vartheta\rangle\geq1-\delta.
    51	\]
    52	Also $\lVert(I-H_W)\vartheta\rVert^2\leq\delta$, whence
    53	\[
    54	  \lVert H_X\vartheta-H_Z\vartheta\rVert^2\leq4\delta.
    55	\]
    56	Together with $H_XH_Z$ equal to the EPR projection, these estimates give the
    57	required overlap bound, with constants absorbed into the stated
    58	$O(\sqrt\delta)$ error.
    59	
    60	For the final transfer, let $\phi\colon\mathcal H\to\mathcal K$ be an isometry
    61	and set $Q=\phi\phi^\dagger$.  If $N_h$ is the unitary-conjugated extension of
    62	a measurement operator $M_h$, then the exact identity is
    63	\[
    64	  \phi M_h\phi^\dagger=N_hQ=QN_h,
    65	\]
    66	not merely $N_h$.  Thus comparison of $N_h$ with an ideal projector must be
    67	combined with control of $(I-Q)\Delta$ on the ideal comparison state
    68	$\Delta$.
    69	
    70	\section{Numerical defects in the source proof}
    71	
    72	Lines~1715--1742 of
    73	\path{references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex}
    74	construct $H_X,H_Z$ and identify $H_XH_Z$ with the EPR projection.  The norm
    75	estimate at lines~1743--1750 gives
    76	$\lVert(I-H_W)\vartheta\rVert\leq\sqrt\delta$.  At lines~1753--1757 the
    77	source substitutes $\delta$ inside the reverse triangle inequality
    78	\cite[lines~1715--1783]{Ji2020MIPStar}.  That replacement is not valid for
    79	small $\delta$.  The desired lower bound on
    80	$\langle H_W^2\rangle$ follows directly from $H_W^2\geq2H_W-I$, as above.
    81	
    82	The triangle inequality yields
    83	\[
    84	  \lVert H_X\vartheta-H_Z\vartheta\rVert\leq2\sqrt\delta,
    85	\]
    86	so its square is at most $4\delta$.  Line~1761 instead bounds that square by
    87	$2\sqrt\delta$ without a stated restriction.  This inequality follows when
    88	$\delta\leq1/4$; for larger error the theorem is made trivial by enlarging the
    89	universal constant.  The same small-error split ensures that the projected
    90	vector defined at lines~1769--1773 is nonzero before it is normalized.  These
    91	are local numerical repairs and do not weaken the extraction conclusion.
    92	
    93	\section{The range-projection obligation}
    94	
    95	Lines~1827--1858 prove state-dependent closeness for the concrete operators
    96	obtained by conjugating the original measurement with the swap unitaries.
    97	Lines~1864--1875 then define isometries by adjoining EPR pairs and applying
    98	those unitaries, and immediately state the corresponding closeness for
    99	$\phi M_h\phi^\dagger$.  The omitted range projection makes this implication
   100	non-definitional \cite[lines~1827--1875]{Ji2020MIPStar}.
   101	
   102	Let $\Psi$ be the original state and suppose $\phi\Psi$ is close to the ideal
   103	state $\Delta$.  Since $Q\phi\Psi=\phi\Psi$ and $Q$ is a contraction, the
   104	triangle inequality bounds $(I-Q)\Delta$ by the state-extraction error.  Using
   105	$\phi M_h\phi^\dagger=N_hQ$, split
   106	\[
   107	  (N_hQ-T_h)\Delta
   108	  =(N_h-T_h)\Delta-N_h(I-Q)\Delta,
   109	\]
   110	where $T_h$ is the ideal Pauli projector.  Summing squared norms over $h$
   111	uses projectivity and orthogonality to keep the second term under control.
   112	The same argument is required for each player and each Pauli basis.
   113	
   114	This transfer is an open proof obligation for the next extraction stage.  It
   115	must be a theorem derived from the concrete swap unitaries, transformed-state
   116	estimate, and operator comparisons.  It must not be stored as a bridge field,
   117	residual assumption, or hypothesis of the source-labelled soundness theorem.
   118	
   119	\section{Blueprint and formalization status}
   120	
   121	The proof of Lemma~\path{lem:qld-unitary} and the soundness proof in
   122	\path{blueprint/src/chapter/ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex} use the corrected
   123	positive-contraction estimate, make the small-error case distinction explicit,
   124	and isolate the range-projection calculation.  The chapter therefore preserves
   125	the source's state and observable conclusions while exposing the omitted
   126	argument.
   127	
   128	The structure \path{ExtractionWitness} in
   129	\path{MIPStarRE/QPBT/Extraction/Unitary.lean} contains only the two-sided
   130	unitarity equations for the concrete swap maps, a normalized auxiliary state,
   131	the transformed-state estimate, and the two-player Pauli-projector comparison.
   132	The theorem \path{exists_extractionWitness_ofGlobalPairWitness} concludes the
   133	existence of this data at the explicit extraction scale, but it takes the
   134	\path{GlobalPairWitness} of Lemma~\path{lem:qld-4-7} as an explicit hypothesis
   135	rather than obtaining it from \path{exists_globalPairWitness}.  That bundle
   136	carries the projective global polynomial-pair measurements and both
   137	point-consistency estimates, and the blueprint proof of
   138	Lemma~\path{lem:qld-unitary} obtains it from Lemma~\path{lem:qld-4-7}; deleting
   139	the hypothesis would leave that construction unproved.  By the criterion of
   140	\path{docs/paper-gaps/proof-gap-protocol.tex} the hypothesis is therefore proof
   141	debt rather than a faithful boundary condition, and the declaration is a
   142	conditional helper: it does not certify the source lemma, and the blueprint

   167	\section{Conclusion}
   168	
   169	The printed triangle calculation has repairable numerical errors, and the
   170	last passage from unitaries to isometries omits a genuine range-projection

    11	\author{}
    12	\date{2026-04-29}

    14	\begin{document}
    15	\maketitle
    16	
    17	\section{Purpose}
    18	
    19	When a formalization relies on a cited mathematical source, the cited source
    20	should remain intact.  It is a source, not an errata file.  If a possible gap,
    21	missing hypothesis, incorrect numerical constant, or other mathematical
    22	discrepancy is found, the matter should be recorded in a separate LaTeX note.
    23	In this repository such notes live under \path{docs/paper-gaps/}.  The same
    24	principle applies when the formal development has already diverged from the
    25	cited source, for instance by changing a statement so that it compiles, or by
    26	using a different mathematical route because an available formal-library theorem
    27	has a slightly different form.  Such a note is a mathematical note first, and a
    28	record of the formalization second: it should be readable by a mathematician or
    29	mathematical physicist who has not followed the issue discussion.
    30	
    31	The note should isolate the mathematical mechanism.  It should say what the
    32	cited source asserts, what the cited results actually imply, where a term or
    33	hypothesis is lost, and what statement the formal development proves instead.
    34	If the formal proof takes a different route, the note should explain the
    35	replacement argument and the hypotheses on which it rests.  This is especially
    36	important when the proof uses a theorem, construction, or convention from
    37	Mathlib which is not part of the cited argument.  In that case the note should
    38	state the Mathlib result in ordinary mathematical language, explain how it is
    39	specialized to the notation of the paper, and compare its hypotheses and
    40	conclusion with the step it replaces.  It should not merely say that \Lean{} did
    41	not accept a proof, that the modified proof compiles, or that a named library
    42	lemma was applied.
    43	
    44	The documents in this directory should themselves follow this standard.  A
    45	policy or template which reads like a checklist will tend to produce checklist
    46	notes; the examples and templates should therefore be written as mathematical
    47	prose.
    48	
    49	\section{Concision and Readability}
    50	
    51	A paper-gap note should be short enough that a reader can understand the issue
    52	in one sitting.  The first page should answer four questions: what the source
    53	uses, how hard the remaining formal work is, what the formalization or audit
    54	checked, and what the current verdict is.  Begin with a short
    55	\emph{At a glance} section when the note concerns an open or recently resolved
    56	formalization task.  That section should estimate the difficulty, the rough
    57	implementation weight, the split between Mathlib reuse and project-local work,
    58	and the key Mathlib APIs or modules.  Use honest ranges, not false precision.
    59	
    60	The \emph{Key theorem forms} section should be Section~2, immediately after
    61	\emph{At a glance}.  Put the theorem forms before the source details so the
    62	reader knows what the formalization is aiming to prove.  After that, keep the
    63	source assertion, the mechanism being checked, the blueprint/formal comparison,
    64	and the conclusion.  Use more sections only when a counterexample or long
    65	derivation genuinely needs room.
    66	
    67	Keep background to the minimum needed for the local point.  Prefer one clear
    68	special case over a general restatement of the surrounding theorem.  Use displayed
    69	equations for the source assertion, the key calculation, and the theorem forms;
    70	avoid displays for traceability data, declaration names, or long lists.  The
    71	blueprint/formal comparison should be compact and should not repeat the theorem
    72	forms.  The section ``Form of the Note'' below specifies where traceability data
    73	belongs; the body should read as mathematical prose, not as a log.
    74	
    75	If the verdict is that there is no mathematical discrepancy, say so plainly and
    76	stop.  Keep the conclusion highly compact, normally under twenty source lines.
    77	If the only remaining work is an implementation task, name it briefly and link
    78	the issue or pull request in a footnote.
    79	
    80	\section{When the Investigation Starts}
    81	
    82	The investigation starts when the obstruction appears to be mathematical rather
    83	than merely formal.  No final judgement is needed at this stage.  It is enough
    84	that, after reading the relevant source and attempting the corresponding formal
    85	statement, the proof seems to require a different scalar, an additional
    86	hypothesis, a different tensor placement, a distinction between two objects which
    87	the prose identifies, or an auxiliary assertion not supplied by the cited
    88	argument.
    89	
    90	The same investigation should also start when such a deviation is discovered
    91	after the fact.  If the existing formal development or informal blueprint has
    92	already changed the statement, strengthened a hypothesis, weakened a conclusion,
    93	inserted an unadvertised lemma, or replaced the cited proof by a different
    94	formal-library argument, the mathematical change should be documented even if all
    95	relevant files already compile.
    96	
    97	At this early stage the purpose is to preserve the question while it is still
    98	local.  The note may later conclude that the matter is only notational, that an
    99	intermediate estimate in the cited source needs a harmless correction, that a
   100	missing hypothesis is genuinely needed, or that no discrepancy remains.  Thus
   101	the trigger is not the severity of the eventual verdict, but the appearance of a
   102	real mismatch between the cited reasoning and the statement that can be
   103	formalized.
   104	
   105	A failed tactic search, a missing formal lemma, or an inconvenient coercion is
   106	not enough.  The obstruction must survive translation back into ordinary
   107	mathematics.
   108	
   109	Sometimes an investigation uncovers an improvement that is not a discrepancy:
   110	the formalization works correctly, but it could be simplified by using an
   111	existing library, replacing a custom type, or adopting a cleaner proof route.
   112	These are not, by themselves, paper-gap notes.  They are action items.  When
   113	such an improvement is identified, open a GitHub issue or pull request that
   114	describes the proposed change.  If the investigation also produces a paper-gap
   115	note, link the issue or pull request from that note: the note records the
   116	mathematical justification, and the issue or pull request drives the
   117	implementation.
   118	
   119	\section{When to Write a Note}
   120	
   121	A note should be written once the source argument and the formal proof no longer
   122	match as mathematical arguments.  This includes, for instance, a numerical
   123	estimate whose constant does not follow from the cited lemma, a displayed
   124	conclusion which uses an unstated hypothesis, or a step in which two objects are
   125	identified although they must remain distinct.  In analytic, algebraic,
   126	probabilistic, or quantum arguments, such distinctions may concern the domain of
   127	a map, the placement of a tensor factor, the type of an outcome, the distinction
   128	between a structure and a substructure, or the scalar carried by an approximation
   129	relation.
   130	
   131	A note is required when an audit finds that a Lean declaration associated with a
   132	source-labelled statement has acquired an extra non-source hypothesis, such as
   133	bridge, residual, repair, producer, or obligation-structure data.  Such a
   134	declaration is temporary proof debt, not a replacement for the source theorem,
   135	and should not be introduced merely to avoid a \verb|sorry|.  The note must say
   136	plainly that the Lean result is conditional, identify the source-faithful theorem
   137	form that remains to be proved, and give the intended obligation discharger or
   138	removal plan.  The blueprint should not mark the source-labelled statement with
   139	\verb|\leanok| by pointing to this conditional helper.
   140	
   141	Changing a Lean theorem away from the statement in
   142	\path{references/ldt-paper/} is strongly discouraged.  A paper-gap note should
   143	not make such a change look routine: it should explain the mathematical
   144	necessity, or else classify the change as proof debt to be removed.
   145	
   146	When an existing conditional helper is audited, the first task is to extract any
   147	argument it already contains into source-faithful lemmas.  If the remaining
   148	bridge hypothesis cannot be derived from the paper hypotheses, the formal
   149	development should restore the source theorem statement and record the missing
   150	proof obligation explicitly, rather than retaining the strengthened statement as
   151	though it were the paper theorem.
   152	
   153	This requirement is not meant to classify every explicit Lean side condition as
   154	a discrepancy.  Positivity, nonemptiness, decidability, field-model instances,
   155	and denominator nonvanishing hypotheses may be faithful encodings of the domain
   156	in which the paper's theorem is stated.  The note should distinguish such
   157	boundary hypotheses from hypotheses that supply an unproved step of the paper
   158	argument.
   159	
   160	A note is also appropriate when the proof becomes formal only after changing an
   161	intermediate scalar, weakening a conclusion, strengthening a hypothesis, or
   162	inserting an additional lemma which is not simply an expansion of the cited
   163	argument.  These are mathematical changes, even when they are harmless for the
   164	final theorem.  It is likewise appropriate when an available formal-library
   165	theorem proves the needed result under a somewhat different formulation from the
   166	cited source.  In that case the note should be deliberately pedagogical.  It
   167	should explain, in ordinary mathematical language, what the replacement result
   168	says, how it is specialized, which hypotheses are new or differently packaged,
   169	and why the resulting statement is a legitimate substitute for the step in the
   170	cited argument.  If the issue remains open after reasonable attempts, the note
   171	should say what has been checked and what remains unknown.
   172	
   173	\section{Counterexamples}
   174	
   175	If the cited assertion appears to be false, the note should not stop at saying
   176	that the proof cannot be formalized.  It should give the counterexample, or the
   177	smallest relevant part of it, in ordinary mathematical notation.  The example
   178	should be accompanied by enough verification that the reader can see both sides:
   179	the hypotheses of the cited assertion hold, and its conclusion fails.
   180	
   181	When feasible, the counterexample should also be formalized in \Lean{}.  This is
   182	especially valuable when the example is finite, algebraic, computational, or
   183	otherwise small enough that the failure can be checked without reproducing the
   184	whole surrounding theory.  The note should then state the mathematical content
   185	of the checked counterexample and identify the corresponding Lean declaration in
   186	a footnote.  The Lean file is not a substitute for the prose: the prose should
   187	still explain why the example refutes the cited assertion.
   188	
   189	\section{Revision of a Note}
   190	
   191	A paper-gap note may be provisional.  It may begin as soon as the mathematical
   192	obstruction has been isolated well enough to state the question, and it may be
   193	revised as the calculation, the blueprint, or the corresponding \Lean{}
   194	declarations become clearer.  The first version need not know the final
   195	classification, but it should say plainly which mathematical point is known and
   196	which point remains unsettled.
   197	
   198	Later revisions should not make the note into a chronological log.  They should
   199	rewrite the document so that it remains a coherent account of the present
   200	mathematical understanding.  If the verdict changes, the conclusion should state
   201	the current verdict; the linked issue or pull request can preserve the earlier
   202	discussion.
   203	
   204	\section{Form of the Note}
   205	
   206	Each note should stand on its own.  It should give the date, cite the relevant
   207	source article, and provide enough traceability for the reader to locate the
   208	original passage and the project discussion.  GitHub issues and pull requests may
   209	be linked with \verb|\href|, and source files, line ranges, and labels should be
   210	recorded when they help the reader check the claim.  These references should
   211	serve the exposition rather than govern it: the main text should be organized
   212	around the mathematical assertion and its proof.
   213	
   214	The note should introduce its notation before using it.  Symbols for
   215	measurements, tensor factors, approximation relations, and error parameters
   216	should be named in prose.  If an approximation relation is state-dependent, the
   217	state should be named, or its defining expression should be given when this can
   218	be done briefly.  Only after the notation is in place should the note state the
   219	assertion in the cited source, using a bibliographic citation such as
   220	\verb|\cite[Section~...]{...}| when the section or chapter is known.

   461	\section{Proof of the soundness of the Pauli basis test}
   462	
   463	We can now prove the soundness theorem for the Pauli basis test, stated as Theorem~\ref{thm:pauli} in Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-test}.
   464	
   465	\begin{proof}
   466		\proves{thm:pauli}
   467		\uses{lem:qld-unitary, lem:qld-extraction-error-form, lem:pauli-completeness,
   468			thm:naimark, lem:projective-strategy-setup, def:expanded-state,
   469			def:EPR, def:povm-distance}
   470		Let $(\ket{\psi},M)$ be a strategy for $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{Pauli}}_{(q,m,d)}$ that succeeds with probability at least $1 - \eps$, where $\ket{\psi}$ is a bipartite state on registers $\mathrm{A}$ and $\mathrm{B}$. By Naimark's theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:naimark}, as formulated in~\cite[Theorem 5.1]{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree}), at the cost of extending $\ket{\psi}$ by sufficiently many ancilla qubits initialized in the state $\ket{0}$, we may assume that the strategy is projective and that the state is padded as in the conventions of Lemma~\ref{lem:projective-strategy-setup} and the convention following it.    471		\[
   472			\phi_{\mathrm{A}}\colon \ket{\theta}_{\mathrm{A}} \mapsto V_{\mathrm{A}} \bigl(\ket{\theta}_{\mathrm{A}} \ot (\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M})_{\mathrm{A}' \mathrm{A}''}\bigr)\;;
   473		\]

   476		% lem:qld-4-7, whose source proof (lines 1277--1413 of
   477		% 14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex) instantiates the classical low
   478		% individual degree test at dimension 2m+2 without a divisibility
   479		% hypothesis; the sentence below records the resulting outstanding
   480		% obligation.

   482		test enters. Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-unitary} rests on the polynomial-pair
   483		measurement of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-7}, whose proof instantiates the

   488		Theorem~\ref{lem:ld-soundness},
   489		is imported from Theorem~4.7 of~\cite{Ji2021Quantum} through an

   492		correspondence nor the bound on the auxiliary parameter of Theorem~4.7 under

   505		$\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}$ appended locally in registers

   510		on registers $\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'$ such that
   511		\[
   512			\bigl\| \phi_{\mathrm{A}} \ot \phi_{\mathrm{B}} \ket{\psi} - \ket{\mathrm{aux}} \ot \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M} \bigr\|^2 \leq \delta_{\mathrm{qld}}\;.
   513		\]

   516		% conjugation estimates of lem:qld-unitary, which concern the

   533		\]

   535		\[
   536			\bigl( \phi_{\mathrm{A}} \, (M^{(\mathrm{Pauli},W)}_h)_{\mathrm{A}} \, \phi_{\mathrm{A}}^\dagger - (\tau^W_h)_{\mathrm{A}''} \bigr) \ket{\Delta}

   551		The proof above, following the source, establishes the first conclusion of Theorem~\ref{thm:pauli} in the squared form $\| \phi_{\mathrm{A}} \ot \phi_{\mathrm{B}} \ket{\psi} - \ket{\mathrm{aux}} \ot \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M} \|^2 \leq \delta_{\mathrm{qld}}$, whereas the theorem bounds the unsquared norm by $\delta_{\mathrm{qld}}(\eps,m,d,q)$.      9	/-!
    10	# The directly indexed low-degree game
    11	
    12	The low-degree game used by the Pauli-basis combining argument is needed in
    13	dimension `2 * m + 2`.  The existing conditionally linear game represents a
    14	coordinate index by an equally sized fiber in the scalar field and therefore
    15	requires the dimension to divide the field size.  This file gives the separate
    16	directly indexed variant which samples that index directly.
    17	
    18	The geometric line carrier records the sampled coordinate, and line evaluation
    19	uses an `Option` outcome rather than assigning a value when a point does not
    20	determine one.  The game retains the point, axis-line, and diagonal-line answer
    21	formats and the nine ordered type branches of the original low-degree game.
    22	
    23	The `Transport` modules relate the direct game to the seed-indexed game and to
    24	the low individual degree test: `Transport.Correspondence`
    25	identifies coordinates, answers, and the question law of the two QPBT
    26	presentations; `Transport.SeedFiber` dilates a seed-indexed strategy to a
    27	direct strategy by a correlated residue register, and `Transport.SeedFiberValue`
    28	shows that the dilation preserves the value exactly; `Transport.Questions`
    29	reads LDT lines as canonical direct questions and rebases direct answers;
    30	`Transport.Strategy` reads one coordinate of a projective direct strategy as a
    31	LDT projective strategy, with exact Born-weight formulas for both constructions;
    32	`Transport.Consistency` reexpresses the three single-polynomial LDT consistency
    33	relations in direct coordinates, the first two at a fixed tuple coordinate; and
    34	`Transport.BranchComparison`, `Transport.DiagonalRecursion`, and
    35	`Transport.PassConversion` convert a value bound of the direct game into the
    36	pass hypothesis of the low individual degree theorem for every
    37	coordinate strategy.  `GameValue` supplies the rejection calculus relating the
    38	direct value to the LDT branch weights.  `Transport.Error` carries the
    39	scalar half of the transport: the auxiliary sampling parameter with which
    40	the low individual degree theorem is applied, bounds on the three terms of its error
    41	function, and the absorption of the resulting simultaneous-measurement
    42	estimate into the error function of `lem:ld-soundness`.
    43	
    44	## References
    45	
    46	The underlying game is `def:ld-game` in
    47	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:17-105`, with source origin
    48	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
    49	The need for the directly indexed repair in Chapter 15 is explained around
    50	`rem:qld-4-7-divisibility` in
    51	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch15_qpbt_combining.tex:1257-1293` and in
    52	`docs/paper-gaps/qpbt_ld-dimension-divisibility.tex`.
    53	-/

    18	\section{At a glance}
    19	
    20	\begin{itemize}
    21	  \item \textbf{Difficulty: medium.}  Two related matters are recorded.
    22	  First, the soundness analysis of the Pauli basis test invokes the
    23	  classical low individual degree game at dimension $2m+2$, and the game's
    24	  question distribution is undefined at that dimension for the admissible
    25	  parameters: it requires $2m+2$ to divide $q$, while admissibility supplies
    26	  only $m \mid q$; the repair is a statement-level reformulation of an
    27	  imported theorem, not a new proof.  Second, the import of the classical
    28	  game's quantum soundness from the tensor-code paper carries two open
    29	  verification obligations at every dimension: the asserted identity with
    30	  the cited tensor-code test is not an identity and must be replaced by a
    31	  reduction with a value bound, and the source's instantiation of the
    32	  theorem's auxiliary parameter violates its lower bound at small
    33	  dimensions (Section~\ref{sec:import-obligations}).
    34	  \item \textbf{Estimated weight:} for the recommended direction, about
    35	  \textbf{3--5 new definitions or interfaces} (a line-point distribution with
    36	  directly sampled index at arbitrary dimension, the directly indexed game,
    37	  and a restated soundness import) plus \textbf{7--10 supporting lemmas},
    38	  including the strategy-transport layer between the directly indexed game
    39	  and the $\chi$-based game (parsing pullback, seed-fiber averaging with
    40	  its open synchronicity-branch control, and a dilation--compression round
    41	  trip of the soundness conclusion); several hundred lines of formal proof.
    42	  Discharging the import obligations of
    43	  Section~\ref{sec:import-obligations} adds the pair-measurement
    44	  construction with its distributional matching, the branch-weight value
    45	  bound, and the parameter-bound case split.  The padding fallback is
    46	  heavier, roughly 6--10 reworked lemmas.
    47	  \item \textbf{Mathlib/project split:} approximately \textbf{15\% Mathlib}
    48	  and \textbf{85\% project-local}.  Mathlib supplies uniform distributions on
    49	  finite types and pushforward identities; the substance is choosing the
    50	  statement of the imported soundness theorem and rechecking the combining
    51	  subtree against it.
    52	  \item \textbf{Key Mathlib inputs:} uniform distributions on finite types
    53	  and their maps, and elementary divisibility arithmetic on powers of two.
    54	  The main inputs are project-local: the classical game, its conditionally
    55	  linear question distribution, and the imported soundness statement.
    56	  Tracked in \localissue{0002}.
    57	\end{itemize}
    58	
    59	\section{Key theorem forms}
    60	
    61	Throughout, $q = 2^k$ with $k$ odd is an admissible field size, the tuple
    62	$(q,m,d)$ is admissible when moreover $d \ge 1$ and $m \mid q$, and
    63	$\mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$ denotes the $m$-variate polynomial representatives
    64	over $\F_q$ of individual degree at most $d$.  The comparison involves four
    65	theorem forms.
    66	\begin{enumerate}
    67	  \item \textbf{Source theorem form} (the polynomial-pair measurement).  There
    68	  is a function $\delta_S(\eps,m,d,q) = a(md)^a(\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})$,
    69	  for universal constants $a > 1$ and $0 < b < 1$, such that for every
    70	  admissible $(q,m,d)$ and every projective strategy for the Pauli basis test
    71	  succeeding with probability at least $1-\eps$, there is a projective
    72	  measurement $\{\hat S_{g_X,g_Z}\}$ with outcomes pairs of polynomials in
    73	  $\mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$ whose evaluations are $\delta_S$-consistent, on
    74	  average over a uniform point $u \in \F_q^m$ and in both bases
    75	  $W \in \{X,Z\}$, with the corresponding points measurements
    76	  $\{\hat M^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_a\}$ of the strategy, together with the
    77	  symmetric counterpart of this relation.
    78	  \item \textbf{Missing instantiation obligation.}  The classical low
    79	  individual degree game with parameter tuple $(q,\, 2m+2,\, d,\, 1)$ is well
    80	  defined, and the combined point and line measurements assembled in the
    81	  analysis constitute a strategy for it of value at least
    82	  $1 - \delta_{\mathrm{combine}}$.  The game's question distribution draws
    83	  its axis and diagonal indices through an index function
    84	  $\chi_{2m+2}\colon \F_q \to \{1,\ldots,2m+2\}$ with classes of equal size
    85	  $q/(2m+2)$, so the game exists only when $2m+2$ divides $q$.
    86	  \item \textbf{Restricted form supported by the present route.}  The source
    87	  theorem form under the additional hypothesis $2m+2 \mid q$.  Among
    88	  admissible tuples this hypothesis holds exactly when $m = 1$ and
    89	  $q \ge 8$; it fails for every admissible tuple with $m \ge 2$ and for
    90	  $(q,m) = (2,1)$.
    91	  \item \textbf{Repaired import form} (recommended target).  Quantum
    92	  soundness of the directly indexed variant of the classical low individual
    93	  degree game over $\F_q^{m'}$, for every dimension $m' \ge 1$ and
    94	  admissible $q$, with no divisibility hypothesis: the question
    95	  distribution samples the axis index, and the diagonal prefix index,
    96	  uniformly from $\{1,\ldots,m'\}$ directly rather than through an index
    97	  function on $\F_q$, and line questions carry the sampled index itself in
    98	  place of the seed $s \in \F_q$; the error is
    99	  $\delta_{\mathrm{ld}}(\eps,q,m',d,k) = a(dm'k)^a(\eps^b + q^{-b} +
   100	  2^{-bm'd})$.  This is a candidate target form, not an established one:
   101	  proving it carries the same two import obligations as the $\chi$-based
   102	  import (Section~\ref{sec:import-obligations}), and deriving the present
   103	  form from it when $m' \mid q$ requires the strategy transport described
   104	  under the candidate repairs below, whose synchronicity step is an open
   105	  obligation.
   106	\end{enumerate}
   107	
   108	\section{The source assertion and the obstruction}
   109	
   110	We examine the final step of the subsection ``Applying the classical
   111	low-degree test'' in the analysis of the Pauli basis test in the compression
   112	paper of Ji, Natarajan, Vidick, Wright, and Yuen (MIP$^{*}$=RE,
   113	arXiv:2001.04383), whose quantum soundness component builds on the low
   114	individual degree test of \cite{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree}.%
   115	\footnote{Tracked in \localissue{0002}.  In the mirror of the source
   116	consulted here, the polynomial-pair lemma and its proof are at
   117	\path{references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex},
   118	lines~1267--1288; the sub-line lemma is at lines~1063--1116 and the combined
   119	line lemma at lines~1020--1034 of the same file.  The game parametrization
   120	with its divisibility, the index function, the soundness statement with its
   121	proof, and admissibility are at
   122	\path{references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex},
   123	lines~33--35, 214--219, 413--458, and 958--961.}
   124	There, the combined point measurements
   125	$\{\hat Q^{x,z,\alpha,\beta}_c\}$ and combined line measurements
   126	$\{\hat Q^{\ell}_f\}$, indexed by points of $\F_q^{2m+2}$ and lines in
   127	$\F_q^{2m+2}$, are asserted to form a strategy for the classical low
   128	individual degree game with parameters
   129	\[
   130	  \mathsf{ldparams} = (q,\, 2m+2,\, d,\, 1)
   131	  \tag{\path{lem:qld-4-7}}
   132	\]
   133	of value $1 - \delta_{\mathrm{combine}}$, and the quantum soundness theorem
   134	for that game is applied to produce the global polynomial-pair measurement.
   135	The two lemmas feeding this step are stated for the line-point distribution
   136	over $\F_q^{2m+2}$.
   137	
   138	The game, however, is parametrized by tuples $(q,m',d,k)$ with $q$ an
   139	admissible field size \emph{and $m'$ dividing $q$}.  The divisibility is not
   140	incidental: the question distribution is a conditionally linear distribution
   141	in which a uniform seed coordinate $s \in \F_q$, read as an integer in
   142	$\{0,\ldots,q-1\}$, determines the axis or diagonal index through the unique
   143	$\chi(s)$ with
   144	\[
   145	  s = (\chi(s)-1)\,\frac{q}{m'} + r, \qquad 0 \le r < \frac{q}{m'},
   146	  \tag{\path{eq:chi-func}}
   147	\]
   148	so that the $m'$ classes $\chi^{-1}(i)$ partition $\F_q$ into sets of equal
   149	size $q/m'$ and the index is uniform.  For $m' \nmid q$ neither the index
   150	function nor the line-point distribution built from it is defined.
   151	
   152	Admissibility of $(q,m,d)$ supplies only $m \mid q$.  Since an admissible $q$
   153	is a power of two, $m \mid q$ forces $m = 2^j$.  For $j \ge 1$ the integer
   154	$m+1 \ge 3$ is odd, so $2m+2 = 2(m+1)$ has an odd factor exceeding $1$ and
   155	divides no power of two; for $m = 1$ the condition $4 \mid q$ holds for every
   156	admissible $q$ except $q = 2$.  Thus the instantiation at dimension $2m+2$ is
   157	undefined for every admissible tuple with $m \ge 2$: for instance
   158	$(q,m,d) = (8,2,1)$ is admissible, while $6 \nmid 8$.  The source performs
   159	the instantiation without addressing the divisibility, so its proof route
   160	establishes the polynomial-pair lemma, and with it the soundness theorem for
   161	the Pauli basis test that rests on it, only for $m = 1$ and $q \ge 8$.
   162	
   163	\section{What the cited soundness theorem requires: the import obligations}
   164	\label{sec:import-obligations}
   165	
   166	The quantum soundness theorem for the classical game inherits the constraint
   167	$m' \mid q$ solely because it is stated for the game just described; its
   168	proof fixes an admissible $q$ with $m' \mid q$, asserts that the game with
   169	simultaneity parameter $1$ is \emph{identical} to the two-prover tensor-code
   170	test for the Reed--Solomon tensor code $\mathcal C^{\ot m'}$ of the same
   171	authors' \emph{Quantum soundness of testing tensor codes} (arXiv:2111.08131)
   172	\cite{Ji2021Quantum}, and concludes by Theorem~4.7 there, instantiated with
   173	that theorem's auxiliary integer parameter --- denoted $k$ in that source,
   174	and written $K$ here to avoid clashing with the field exponent and the
   175	simultaneity parameter --- chosen as $(m')^3 d$.  Neither
   176	the asserted identity nor the instantiation is complete as stated, so the
   177	import carries two verification obligations, which this section details and
   178	which the blueprint's proof node for the soundness statement records as
   179	open.  Both obligations are independent of the divisibility question: they
   180	arise at every dimension, for the $\chi$-based game where it is defined and
   181	equally for the directly indexed variant proposed under the candidate
   182	repairs.
   183	
   184	\paragraph{The cited test.}
   185	In the two-prover tensor-code test (Figures~1 and~2 of
   186	\cite{Ji2021Quantum}; the two-prover strategy format and the goodness
   187	measure are Definitions~4.5 and~4.6 there), the referee performs one of
   188	three subtests with probability $1/3$ each, assigning the two roles of each
   189	subtest to the two provers uniformly at random.  \emph{Axis-parallel lines
   190	test}: sample a uniform point $u \in [n]^{m'}$ and a uniform axis
   191	$j \in \{1,\ldots,m'\}$; send the axis-parallel line $\ell$ through $u$ in
   192	direction $j$ to one prover, who answers a codeword $g \in \mathcal C$;
   193	send $u$ to the other, who answers a field value $a$; accept iff
   194	$g(u_j) = a$.  \emph{Subcube commutation test}: sample
   195	$j \in \{1,\ldots,m'\}$ and a subcube $H \subseteq [n]^{m'}$ by fixing the
   196	last $j-1$ coordinates uniformly; sample $u, v$ independently and uniformly
   197	in $H$ and a uniform order bit; send the ordered pair $(u,v)$ or $(v,u)$ to
   198	one prover, who answers a pair $(b_u, b_v)$ of field values; send $u$ to
   199	the other, who answers $a$; accept iff $b_u = a$.  \emph{Synchronicity
   200	test}: send one identical question --- a line, a point, or an ordered
   201	pair, with probability $1/3$ each --- to both provers and accept iff their
   202	answers agree.  Theorem~4.7 supposes a two-prover strategy passing this
   203	test with probability $1-\eps$ together with an integer parameter
   204	$K \ge 12 m' t$, where $t$ is the interpolation parameter of the base code
   205	--- for the degree-$d$ Reed--Solomon code, of blocklength $n = q$ and
   206	distance $q-d$, one has $t = d+1$ --- and produces projective measurements
   207	$\{G_c\}$ and $\{\tilde G_c\}$ with outcomes in $\mathcal C^{\ot m'}$,
   208	consistent with one prover's points measurements, with the other prover's
   209	lines measurements, and with each other, up to
   210	$\eta'(m',t,K,\eps,n^{-1}) = \mathrm{poly}(m',t,K) \cdot
   211	\mathrm{poly}(\eps, n^{-1}, e^{-K/(m')^2})$.
   212	
   213	\paragraph{Obligation 1: the game correspondence.}
   214	The source asserts that the $\chi$-based game at parameters $(q,m',d,1)$
   215	is this test.  It is not, in four respects.
   216	(i)~The game has no pair questions.  A pair question of the test reveals
   217	two points of a \emph{hidden} subcube --- the subcube itself is not sent
   218	--- and is answered by two field values, while the game's diagonal-line
   219	question reveals a full line description and is answered by a degree-$m'd$
   220	polynomial.  A reduction must construct the pair measurements from the
   221	diagonal-line measurements by post-processing (measure a line through $u$
   222	and $v$ and evaluate the answered polynomial at the two parameters), and
   223	both directions of the information mismatch matter: the game's line
   224	description carries an index and a seed, neither of which is a function of
   225	the pair $(u,v)$, so the constructed measurement must average over the
   226	compatible indices and seeds; and the game's diagonal lines fix the
   227	\emph{first} $i-1$ coordinates where the test's subcubes fix the
   228	\emph{last} $j-1$, so the coordinate conventions must be aligned.  The
   229	construction must preserve projectivity and must match the law of the
   230	hidden-subcube pair with the law induced by the game's diagonal sampling.
   231	(ii)~The game's line questions carry the seed $s \in \F_q$; the test's
   232	carry only the line.  A strategy may depend on the seed beyond its class
   233	$\chi^{-1}(i)$, and removing this dependence runs into the fiber-averaging
   234	difficulty made explicit under the candidate repairs: averaging preserves
   235	the line-versus-point branches exactly but not the synchronicity branches.
   236	(iii)~The branch weights differ: each nontrivial cross-test has mass $1/3$
   237	in the test against $2/9$ in the game.  Once the per-branch predicates are
   238	matched, the intended bookkeeping bound is that the constructed strategy's
   239	rejection probability in the test is at most $\tfrac32$ times the game's
   240	rejection probability, up to the $O(1/(m'q))$ of item~(iv); this bound is
   241	the target of the obligation, not an established fact.
   242	(iv)~The game's predicate fixes an acceptance convention on diagonal
   243	questions with zero direction --- an event of probability at most
   244	$2/(m'q)$, recorded in the blueprint's remark on zero directions --- for
   245	which the test has no counterpart branch.
   246	Finally, the displayed conclusions of Theorem~4.7 pair one prover's points
   247	measurements with the other prover's tensor-codeword measurement, and the
   248	first prover's tensor-codeword measurement with the second prover's lines
   249	measurements, while the game-level statement asserts the point consistency
   250	in both directions; deriving the stated form uses the role symmetrization
   251	of the test and belongs to the correspondence.  None of these steps is
   252	difficult to state, but none is carried out in the source, and together
   253	they replace the asserted one-line identity by a reduction carrying its
   254	own value bound.
   255	
   256	\paragraph{Obligation 2: the parameter bound.}
   257	Theorem~4.7 requires $K \ge 12 m' t = 12 m' (d+1)$.  The source
   258	instantiates $K = (m')^3 d$, which meets the bound iff
   259	$(m')^2 d \ge 12(d+1)$: this holds for all $d \ge 1$ when $m' \ge 5$,
   260	holds at $m' = 4$ exactly when $d \ge 3$, and fails for every $d$ when
   261	$m' \le 3$.  In the game's parameter domain the dimension divides the
   262	admissible field size and is therefore a power of two, so the source's
   263	instantiation violates the hypothesis exactly at $m' \in \{1,2\}$ for
   264	every $d$ and at $m' = 4$ for $d \in \{1,2\}$ --- in particular, in the
   265	multilinear regime $d = 1$, at every dimension $m' \le 4$.  A candidate
   266	repair is to instantiate $K = \max((m')^3 d,\, 12 m'(d+1))$; the open
   267	obligation is then to re-absorb the error, that is, to check that
   268	$\mathrm{poly}(m',t,K)$ and $e^{-K/(m')^2}$ still collapse to the form
   269	$a(dm')^a(\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bm'd})$ in the small-$m'$ cases where the
   270	maximum is $12m'(d+1)$ --- plausible, since there
   271	$e^{-K/(m')^2} = e^{-12(d+1)/m'}$ decays in $d$ at a rate comparable to
   272	$2^{-m'd}$ for $m' \le 4$, but not checked here.
   273	
   274	In the correspondence of Obligation~1, the only role of the divisibility
   275	$m' \mid q$ is to make the $\chi$-sampled index uniform.  The underlying
   276	mathematics does not need the divisibility.  The low
   277	individual degree test of \cite{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree} samples its axis
   278	index $i$ uniformly from $\{1,\ldots,m'\}$ directly, with no index function
   279	on $\F_q$ and no divisibility hypothesis,%
   280	\footnote{See the test figure in \path{references/ldt-paper/test_definition.tex}.}

    17	\section{Purpose}
    18	
    19	This note fixes terminology for a recurring failure mode in the formalization
    20	of the low individual degree test paper, \path{arXiv:2009.12982}.  It
    21	complements the note-writing policy in \path{docs/paper-gaps/policy.tex} and
    22	the source-statement audit tracked historically in \ghissue{1458}.  The current
    23	source-boundary proof holes are tracked in \ghissue{1507} and \ghissue{422}.
    24	A proof may be blocked at
    25	an intermediate mathematical assertion.  If that assertion is added as a new
    26	hypothesis to a theorem labelled as a paper theorem, the resulting \Lean{}
    27	theorem
    28	may be correct as a conditional statement, but it is no longer the theorem in
    29	the cited source.  The apparent proof has not closed the paper theorem; it has
    30	moved a proof obligation into the theorem statement.
    31	
    32	The protocol below distinguishes such proof debt from legitimate formal
    33	boundary conditions and from genuine mathematical corrections.  It is meant for
    34	contributors and reviewers who must decide whether a bridge, residual, repair,
    35	input, or obligation structure is a proved local construction, a tracked proof
    36	gap, or statement drift which must be repaired before a theorem may be
    37	advertised as a source theorem.  The default rule is restrictive: such data
    38	must not be added to a paper-facing theorem unless it is part of the cited
    39	source statement or a documented faithful encoding of its ambient hypotheses.
    40	
    41	\section{Basic objects}
    42	
    43	\paragraph{Source theorem.}
    44	A source theorem is a theorem, lemma, proposition, or corollary in the paper
    45	source under \path{references/ldt-paper/}.  Its hypotheses and conclusion are
    46	the mathematical ground truth, subject only to faithful formal encoding and to
    47	documented paper-gap corrections.
    48	
    49	\paragraph{Paper-facing declaration.}
    50	A \Lean{} declaration is paper-facing when it is named or cited as the
    51	formalization of a source theorem, for instance through a blueprint
    52	\verb|\lean{}| link on a theorem environment carrying a paper label.  Such a
    53	declaration must match the source theorem in its public statement.  In
    54	particular, it may not add an unproved bridge, residual, repair, input,
    55	obligation structure, or other proof-obligation hypothesis which the paper does
    56	not assume.
    57	
    58	\paragraph{Proof obligation.}
    59	A proof obligation is an intermediate assertion needed by the proof of a source
    60	theorem.  It may be a construction, an estimate, a transport lemma, or a
    61	comparison between two formal representations.  If the paper proves or invokes
    62	this assertion, then the formalization should state it as a separate lemma or
    63	theorem and prove it from the upstream hypotheses.
    64	
    65	\paragraph{Obligation discharger.}
    66	An obligation discharger is a theorem or definition which constructs a proof
    67	obligation from the paper hypotheses already available at that point in the
    68	argument.  This is the preferred representation of missing work.  If the proof
    69	is not yet complete, the discharger may temporarily contain a tracked
    70	\verb|sorry|, but the paper-facing theorem should call it rather than assume
    71	its output as an additional theorem hypothesis.
    72	
    73	\paragraph{Conditional helper.}
    74	A conditional helper is a separately named theorem whose statement explicitly
    75	assumes a proof obligation.  Names such as
    76	\leanid{mainFormal\_ofInternalObligations},
    77	\leanid{orthonormalization\_ofInput}, or names whose suffix advertises the
    78	assumed obligation are permitted only when the declaration is not presented as
    79	the source theorem.  A conditional helper is a quarantine for downstream proof
    80	content; it does not close the source theorem.
    81	
    82	\section{Bridge, residual, repair, input, and obligation structures}
    83	
    84	The words \emph{bridge}, \emph{residual}, \emph{repair}, \emph{input}, and
    85	\emph{obligation structure} name possible formal shapes.  They become dangerous
    86	when their mathematical status is unclear or when their names make unproved
    87	data look like acceptable hypotheses of a source theorem.
    88	
    89	\paragraph{Bridge.}
    90	A bridge should be a transport theorem between two already defined
    91	mathematical forms: for example, a tensor-placement identity, a conversion
    92	between two equivalent consistency relations, or a statement translating a
    93	source object into a formal representation.  A bridge is harmless only after it
    94	is proved from previously available assumptions.  It becomes proof debt when it
    95	is assumed because the transport has not yet been proved.  It becomes theorem
    96	drift when the assumed bridge is added to a paper-facing theorem.
    97	
    98	\paragraph{Residual.}
    99	A residual is a named remainder after part of an argument has been performed.
   100	It is often a useful way to record the exact missing target after a completed
   101	construction.  A residual may appear as the conclusion of a helper theorem or
   102	as the input of a quarantined conditional helper.  It is not a permissible new
   103	assumption on a paper theorem unless the paper itself assumes that residual.
   104	
   105	\paragraph{Input.}
   106	An input is a named bundle of data or hypotheses consumed by a construction or
   107	conditional helper.  It is harmless only when each load-bearing field is either
   108	part of the source hypotheses or is produced by an earlier theorem.  It becomes
   109	proof debt when the bundle is merely assumed because the construction of its
   110	fields is missing.  It becomes theorem drift when such a bundle is added to the
   111	public statement of a source theorem.
   112	
   113	\paragraph{Repair.}
   114	A repair is a mathematical construction which replaces an approximate or
   115	partial object by a better object, usually with a quantitative estimate.  In
   116	the low individual degree test formalization, projectivization and
   117	orthonormalization repairs are genuine mathematical operations.  A repair
   118	should therefore appear as a construction or as a theorem discharging the
   119	corresponding obligation.  If a theorem assumes the output of the repair instead
   120	of constructing it, that theorem is conditional on the repair.
   121	
   122	\paragraph{Obligation structure.}
   123	An obligation structure is a record whose fields are the data and estimates
   124	needed by a later construction.  This is acceptable only as an internal target
   125	or as a hypothesis of a conditional helper.  Such a structure becomes statement
   126	drift if it is added to a paper-facing theorem instead of being constructed
   127	inside the proof.  The review question is whether every load-bearing field is
   128	proved from the source hypotheses or is explicitly tracked as a missing
   129	obligation.
   130	
   131	\section{The main failure mode}
   132	
   133	Suppose the paper proves
   134	\[
   135	  H \Longrightarrow C.
   136	\]
   137	During formalization, the proof may need an intermediate assertion \(B\).  The
   138	paper theorem should be represented as
   139	\[
   140	  H \Longrightarrow B \Longrightarrow C
   141	  \quad\text{inside the proof,}
   142	\]
   143	where \(B\) is obtained by a lemma or theorem from \(H\).  The following
   144	public statement is a different theorem:
   145	\[
   146	  H \land B \Longrightarrow C.
   147	\]
   148	It is not unsound in \Lean{}, but it is not the paper theorem.  It says that the
   149	conclusion follows if the missing bridge data is supplied.  Such a theorem is a
   150	conditional helper, even if its conclusion looks exactly like the paper's
   151	conclusion.
   152	
   153	This is the situation colloquially described as ``adding a bridge
   154	hypothesis''.  More precisely, an unproved intermediate step has been promoted
   155	from the proof body to the theorem's assumptions.  The correction is not to hide
   156	the hypothesis under a different structure name.  The correction is to keep a
   157	paper-facing theorem with the source statement and move the missing step to a
   158	named internal proof obligation.
   159	
   160	\section{Faithful boundary hypotheses}
   161	
   162	Not every extra formal hypothesis is a theorem drift.  Some hypotheses are
   163	faithful boundary conditions introduced by formal encoding.  Examples include
   164	nonnegativity needed for a real power, positivity needed to divide by a
   165	quantity, finiteness and nonemptiness of an index type, a field-model instance,
   166	or decidability instances required by \Lean{}.  Such hypotheses are acceptable
   167	when they express part of the mathematical ambient setting or make explicit a
   168	condition used implicitly in the paper.
   169	
   170	The distinction is load-bearing.  A faithful boundary hypothesis describes the
   171	domain in which the paper's objects live.  A proof-debt hypothesis supplies a
   172	mathematical step that the proof should derive.  If removing the hypothesis
   173	leaves an unproved construction or estimate from the paper proof, then the
   174	hypothesis is proof debt, not a boundary condition.
   175	
   176	\section{Definition drift and subtree repair}
   177	
   178	Definition drift is especially dangerous because it propagates.  If a
   179	definition is changed so that it no longer denotes the object in the paper,
   180	then every downstream theorem using that definition may continue to compile
   181	while proving statements about the wrong object.  Downstream theorem statements
   182	can then be repaired piecemeal, but the development remains unstable because
   183	the wrong definition is still upstream.
   184	
   185	When a definition mismatch is found, the repair should proceed by a subtree
   186	protocol.
   187	
   188	\begin{enumerate}
   189	  \item Identify the source object and the formal object precisely.
   190	  \item Freeze a source-faithful definition or state an adapter theorem
   191	  relating the existing definition to the source object.
   192	  \item Recheck the downstream theorem chain against that definition or adapter.
   193	  \item Re-formalize the affected subtree from the corrected interface, rather
   194	  than adding local hypotheses to each downstream theorem.
   195	  \item If a downstream proof cannot be completed, record the missing obligation
   196	  at the lowest point where the paper proof needs it.
   197	\end{enumerate}
   198	
   199	This is slower than editing a final theorem signature, but it prevents a local
   200	definition error from becoming a global theorem-statement error.
   201	
   202	\section{Allowed shapes}
   203	
   204	\begin{center}
   205	\begin{tabular}{p{0.24\linewidth}p{0.31\linewidth}p{0.32\linewidth}}
   206	\textbf{Shape} & \textbf{Allowed use} & \textbf{Forbidden use} \\
   207	\hline
   208	Paper-facing theorem & Matches the source statement up to faithful encoding &
   209	Carries non-paper bridge, residual, repair, input, obligation-structure, or
   210	proof-obligation hypotheses \\
   211	Source-shaped theorem with a tracked \verb|sorry| & Default repair when the
   212	source proof is blocked but the statement is known & Replaced by a strengthened
   213	theorem statement merely to keep the file compiling \\
   214	Conditional helper & Temporary quarantine for substantial proof content whose
   215	remaining named obligation has not yet been discharged & Introduced merely to
   216	avoid a \verb|sorry|, or linked as the source theorem or marked as
   217	proof-complete for that theorem \\
   218	Obligation discharger theorem & Constructs the obligation from paper hypotheses &
   219	Merely restates the obligation as an assumption \\
   220	Input bundle & Collects produced data for a local construction & Is assumed by a
   221	source theorem instead of being produced \\
   222	Obligation structure & Bundles constructed data and estimates & Hides unproved
   223	fields that are then assumed by a source theorem \\
   224	Paper-gap note & Documents a real mathematical or formal-statement divergence &
   225	Justifies silent statement drift without a repair plan
   226	\end{tabular}

   231	When a source-labelled proof is blocked, use the following order.
   232

   237	  first missing intermediate assertion.
   238	  \item Decide whether the missing assertion is a faithful boundary condition,
   239	  a representation adapter, an ordinary lemma from the paper proof, or a real
   240	  paper-gap discrepancy.
   241	  \item If it is an ordinary lemma or adapter, create a named theorem which
   242	  discharges that obligation.  Do not add it to the source theorem as a new
   243	  hypothesis.
   244	  \item Keep the source-labelled theorem itself in the source form, even if its

   246	  the missing assertion has not yet been proved.
   247	  \item Create a conditional helper only to quarantine substantial proof content

   249	  merely to avoid a \verb|sorry| or to keep making progress.  If a conditional
   250	  helper remains, give it a conditional name, keep it separate from the

   256	  declarations.  Conditional helpers belong in remarks or implementation
   257	  notes, not in the source theorem block.

   172	/-! ## The subline distribution -/
   173	
   174	/-- A tuple consisting of an extended line and its projected X and Z lines. -/
   175	abbrev SubLineTriple (P : AdmissibleParams) :=
   176	  DirectLineDesc P.extendedDirectLd ×
   177	    (LineDesc P.toLdParams × LineDesc P.toLdParams)
   178	
   179	/-- An extended line tuple together with a point sampled uniformly on it. -/
   180	abbrev SubLinePointSample (P : AdmissibleParams) :=
   181	  SubLineTriple P ×
   182	    (Fin P.extendedDirectLd.m -> DirectScalarQ P.extendedDirectLd)
   183	
   184	/-- The shared restricted line kind and two coordinate indices in one mixture
   185	component of the subline law. -/
   186	abbrev SubLineComponent (P : AdmissibleParams) :=
   187	  LineKind × (Fin P.m × Fin P.m)
   188	
   189	/-- Select the restricted line-point distribution of a given kind and index. -/
   190	noncomputable def restrictedLinePointDist (P : AdmissibleParams)
   191	    (kind : LineKind) (i : Fin P.m) :
   192	    Distribution (LineDesc P.toLdParams × (Fin P.m -> PauliScalar P)) :=
   193	  match kind with
   194	  | .axis => restrictedALineDist P.toLdParams i
   195	  | .diagonal => restrictedDLineDist P.toLdParams i
   196	
   197	/-- Sample a subline tuple and then a uniform affine parameter on its
   198	extended line. -/
   199	noncomputable def subLinePointDist (P : AdmissibleParams)
   200	    (D : Distribution (SubLineTriple P)) :
   201	    Distribution (SubLinePointSample P) :=
   202	  (Distribution.prod D
   203	    (uniformDistribution (DirectScalarQ P.extendedDirectLd))).map fun sample =>
   204	      (sample.1, sample.1.1.base + sample.2 • sample.1.1.direction)
   205	
   206	/-- Retain the projected line pair and the X projection of an extended point. -/
   207	def subLineXProjection {P : AdmissibleParams} (sample : SubLinePointSample P) :
   208	    (LineDesc P.toLdParams × LineDesc P.toLdParams) ×
   209	      (Fin P.m -> PauliScalar P) :=
   210	  (sample.1.2, projX (directPointToPauli P sample.2))
   211	
   212	/-- Retain the projected line pair and the Z projection of an extended point. -/
   213	def subLineZProjection {P : AdmissibleParams} (sample : SubLinePointSample P) :
   214	    (LineDesc P.toLdParams × LineDesc P.toLdParams) ×
   215	      (Fin P.m -> PauliScalar P) :=
   216	  (sample.1.2, projZ (directPointToPauli P sample.2))
   217	
   218	/-- The X-point marginal associated with one restricted product component. -/
   219	noncomputable def subLineXComponentDist (P : AdmissibleParams)
   220	    (component : SubLineComponent P) :
   221	    Distribution
   222	      ((LineDesc P.toLdParams × LineDesc P.toLdParams) ×
   223	        (Fin P.m -> PauliScalar P)) :=
   224	  (Distribution.prod
   225	    (restrictedLinePointDist P component.1 component.2.1)
   226	    ((restrictedLinePointDist P component.1 component.2.2).map Prod.fst)).map
   227	      fun sample => ((sample.1.1, sample.2), sample.1.2)
   228	
   229	/-- The Z-point marginal associated with one restricted product component. -/
   230	noncomputable def subLineZComponentDist (P : AdmissibleParams)
   231	    (component : SubLineComponent P) :
   232	    Distribution
   233	      ((LineDesc P.toLdParams × LineDesc P.toLdParams) ×
   234	        (Fin P.m -> PauliScalar P)) :=
   235	  (Distribution.prod
   236	    ((restrictedLinePointDist P component.1 component.2.1).map Prod.fst)
   237	    (restrictedLinePointDist P component.1 component.2.2)).map
   238	      fun sample => ((sample.1, sample.2.1), sample.2.2)
   239	
   240	/-- The subline distribution of `lem:qld-sublines`, paper lines 1063--1069.
   241	Its source-mixture field records the X and Z point marginals separately; it
   242	does not assert a joint conditional law for the pair of projected points. -/
   243	structure SubLineWitness (P : AdmissibleParams) where
   244	  /-- The actual distribution of an extended line and two projected lines. -/
   245	  D : Distribution (SubLineTriple P)
   246	  /-- The distribution has total mass one. -/
   247	  isProbability : D.IsProbability
   248	  /-- Its extended-line marginal is the direct line-point marginal. -/
   249	  extended_marginal : D.map Prod.fst =
   250	    (directLinePointDist P.extendedDirectLd).map Prod.fst
   251	  /-- Every point of an extended line projects onto both stored source lines. -/
   252	  incidence : ∀ sample ∈ D.support, ∀ u ∈ sample.1.pointSet,
   253	    projX (directPointToPauli P u) ∈ sample.2.1.pointSet ∧
   254	      projZ (directPointToPauli P u) ∈ sample.2.2.pointSet
   255	  /-- Each line triple carries affine data sufficient for
   256	  `combineLinePoly_spec`. -/
   257	  compatibility : ∀ sample ∈ D.support,
   258	    ∃ aX bX aZ bZ uAlpha vAlpha uBeta vBeta : PauliScalar P,
   259	      IsCombineLineCompatible
   260	        (directPointToPauli P sample.1.base)
   261	        (directPointToPauli P sample.1.direction)
   262	        sample.2.1.base sample.2.1.direction
   263	        sample.2.2.base sample.2.2.direction
   264	        aX bX aZ bZ uAlpha vAlpha uBeta vBeta
   265	  /-- Each one-point projected marginal is a mixture of restricted product
   266	  laws.  No equality for their joint conditional law is claimed. -/
   267	  source_mixture : ∃ components : Distribution (SubLineComponent P),
   268	    components.IsProbability ∧
   269	      (subLinePointDist P D).map subLineXProjection =
   270	        Distribution.bind components (subLineXComponentDist P) ∧
   271	      (subLinePointDist P D).map subLineZProjection =
   272	        Distribution.bind components (subLineZComponentDist P)
   273	  /-- An extended axis line has axis-parallel projected lines. -/
   274	  axis_closure : ∀ sample ∈ D.support, sample.1.kind = .axis ->
   275	    sample.2.1.kind = .axis ∧ sample.2.2.kind = .axis
   276	
   277	/-! ## Extended lines and global polynomial pairs -/
   278	
   279	/-- Extended-line POVMs and directly indexed, completed-answer forms of the two
   280	consistency relations in `lem:qld-4-13`, paper lines 1020--1034. The direct line
   281	carrier avoids the dimension-divisibility obstruction documented in
   282	`docs/paper-gaps/qpbt_ld-dimension-divisibility.tex`. -/
   283	structure ExtendedLinesWitness {P : AdmissibleParams} {ε δQ : ℝ}
   284	    (S : ProjectiveSetting P ε) (points : CombinedPointsWitness S δQ)
   285	    (δ : ℝ) where
   286	  /-- The complete extended-line measurement on each player side. -/
   287	  Qline : (side : PlayerSide) -> DirectLineDesc P.extendedDirectLd ->
   288	    Measurement (DirectDegPoly P.extendedDirectLd (P.m * P.d + 1))
   289	      (S.ExpandedLocalSpace side)
   290	  /-- Axis-line outcomes outside degree `d` have zero effect. -/
   291	  axis_degree : ∀ side line f, line.kind = .axis ->
   292	    Not (∀ i, P.d < i.val -> f i = 0) ->
   293	      (Qline side line).effect f = 0
   294	  /-- Alice's evaluated line measurement is consistent with Bob's completed
   295	  combined point measurement. -/
   296	  consistent_alice : consistencyDefect
   297	    (directLinePointDist P.extendedDirectLd)
   298	    (fun sample answer => S.place .AA'
   299	      (((Qline .alice sample.1).postprocess

   308	    S.psiHat <= δ
   309	  /-- Bob's evaluated line measurement is consistent with Alice's completed
   310	  combined point measurement. -/
   311	  consistent_bob : consistencyDefect
   312	    (directLinePointDist P.extendedDirectLd)
   313	    (fun sample answer => S.place .BB'
   314	      (((Qline .bob sample.1).postprocess
   315	        (fun f => (directEvalOpt sample.1 sample.2 f).map
   316	          (extendedDirectScalarEquiv P))).effect answer))
   317	    (fun sample answer => S.place .AB''
   318	      (((points.Q .alice
   319	        (projX (directPointToPauli P sample.2))
   320	        (projZ (directPointToPauli P sample.2))).postprocess fun ab =>
   321	          some (directPointToPauli P sample.2 (alphaVar P.m) * ab.1 +
   322	            directPointToPauli P sample.2 (betaVar P.m) * ab.2)).effect answer))
   323	    S.psiHat <= δ

 /-! ## The canonical scalar identification -/
 
 /-- Identify the direct extended game's scalar field with the Pauli scalar
 field.  Both are selected by `fixedFieldModel`; only their proof argument for
 admissibility differs. -/
 noncomputable def extendedDirectScalarEquiv (P : AdmissibleParams) :
     DirectScalarQ P.extendedDirectLd ≃+* PauliScalar P := by
   have h : P.extendedDirectLd.hq = P.hq := Subsingleton.elim _ _
   cases h
   exact RingEquiv.refl _
 
 /-- Transport an extended direct point into the canonical Pauli scalar field. -/
 def directPointToPauli (P : AdmissibleParams)
     (u : Fin P.extendedDirectLd.m -> DirectScalarQ P.extendedDirectLd) :
     Fin (2 * P.m + 2) -> PauliScalar P :=
   fun i => extendedDirectScalarEquiv P (u i)
 
 /-! ## Finite direct-line carrier -/
 
 /-- A finite code for directly indexed lines, omitting only proof fields. -/
 private abbrev DirectLineDescCode (D : DirectLdParams) :=
   ((Fin D.m -> DirectScalarQ D) × Fin D.m) ⊕
     ((Fin D.m -> DirectScalarQ D) × Fin D.m ×
       (Fin D.m -> DirectScalarQ D))
 
 /-- Encode a directly indexed line by its tag and mathematical data. -/
 private def directLineDescCode (D : DirectLdParams) :
     DirectLineDesc D -> DirectLineDescCode D
   | .axis base index _ => .inl (base, index)
   | .diagonal base index direction _ _ => .inr (base, index, direction)
 
 /-- The direct-line code is injective by proof irrelevance. -/
 private theorem directLineDescCode_injective (D : DirectLdParams) :
     Function.Injective (directLineDescCode D) := by
   intro line line' h
   cases line with
   | axis base index baseFixed =>
       cases line' with
       | axis base' index' baseFixed' =>
           simp only [directLineDescCode, Sum.inl.injEq, Prod.mk.injEq] at h
           rcases h with ⟨rfl, rfl⟩
           rfl
       | diagonal => simp [directLineDescCode] at h
   | diagonal base index direction baseFixed prefixZero =>
       cases line' with
       | axis => simp [directLineDescCode] at h
       | diagonal base' index' direction' baseFixed' prefixZero' =>
           simp only [directLineDescCode, Sum.inr.injEq, Prod.mk.injEq] at h
           rcases h with ⟨rfl, rfl, rfl⟩
           rfl

 noncomputable instance directLineDescFintype (D : DirectLdParams) :
     Fintype (DirectLineDesc D) :=
   Fintype.ofInjective (directLineDescCode D) (directLineDescCode_injective D)

     (δ : ℝ) where

     (fun sample answer => S.place .BB'
       (((Qline .bob sample.1).postprocess

         (((Smeas .alice).postprocess (evalAt W u)).effect a))
       (fun u a => S.place .BA''
         ((S.pointMeasExp .bob W u).effect a))
       S.psiHat <= δ
   /-- Bob's global evaluations are consistent with Alice's source point
   measurements, for each Pauli basis. -/
   point_consistent_bob : ∀ W : PauliKind,
     consistencyDefect (uniformDistribution (Fin P.m -> PauliScalar P))
       (fun u a => S.place .BB'
         (((Smeas .bob).postprocess (evalAt W u)).effect a))
       (fun u a => S.place .AB''
         ((S.pointMeasExp .alice W u).effect a))
       S.psiHat <= δ

 	exists an isomorphism $\phi : (\C^q)^{\ot L} \to (\C^2)^{\ot Lk}$ such that
 	\begin{equation}\label{eq:epr-q-to-epr-2}
 		\phi \ot \phi\, \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot L}
 		= \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}^{\ot Lk}

 	(applying the natural identifications between
 	$(\C^q)^{\ot L} \ot (\C^q)^{\ot L}$ and $(\C^q \ot \C^q)^{\ot L}$, and

 \section{Combined point measurements}
 
 The measurements $\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},X),x}$ and
 $\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},Z),z}$ commute only approximately. The first goal of
 this chapter is to construct a single projective measurement that
 simultaneously measures both, first at points and then along lines. The
 construction of the combined point measurement proceeds in three steps: the
 binary refinements $\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},X),x,r}$ and
 $\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},Z),z,s}$ are combined into a sandwich POVM, the
 resulting family is shown to satisfy an approximate linearity in the index
 pair $(r,s)$, and the following result of Natarajan and
 Vidick~\cite{Natarajan2017Linearity} converts approximate linearity into exact
 linearity, from which a projective measurement with outcomes in $\F_q^2$ is
 assembled by Fourier averaging.

 This chapter completes the analysis of the Pauli basis test~\cite{Ji2020MIPStar}. Throughout, $(q,m,d)$ is an admissible parameter tuple (Definition~\ref{def:admissible}), $q = 2^t$, and $M = 2^m$ denotes the number of $q$-ary qudits tested for per player. (The letter $M$ also denotes measurement operators, always carrying super- and subscripts; the meaning is determined by context, as in the source.) We fix a projective strategy for the Pauli basis test game $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{Pauli}}_{(q,m,d)}$ that succeeds with probability at least $1-\eps$, in the setting of Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-observables}: the shared state $\ket{\psi}$ on registers $\mathrm{A}$, $\mathrm{B}$ is assumed padded with sufficiently many ancilla qubits in the state $\ket{0}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:projective-strategy-setup} and the convention following it), and $\ket{\hat\psi}$ denotes the expanded state on the six registers $\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{A}''\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'\mathrm{B}''$, obtained by adjoining to each player the two halves of $M$ pairs $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}$ (Definition~\ref{def:expanded-state}). Unless stated otherwise, every $\approx_\delta$ and $\simeq_\delta$ statement below is taken with respect to the state $\ket{\hat\psi}$, over the question distribution named in the statement, with register placements indicated by subscripts; ``all symmetric equivalents'' refers to the register interchanges of Definition~\ref{def:symmetric-equivalents}.
 
 We use the following objects from the preceding chapters: the combined point projectors $\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_a$ acting on the expanded space (Definition~\ref{def:expanded-point-measurement}); the projective polynomial-pair measurement $\{\hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z}\}$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-7}, with outcomes pairs of polynomials in $\mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$ and error function
 \[
 	\delta_G(\eps,m,d,q) = a(md)^a\bigl(\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd}\bigr)
 \]
 for universal constants $a > 1$, $0 < b < 1$. This is the error denoted $\delta_S$ in Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-7}; we call it $\delta_G$ here to distinguish the global polynomial-pair witness error from the enlarged error used below. We also use the decoding map $\mathrm{Dec} = \mathrm{Dec}_{\F_q}\colon \mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q) \to \F_q^{M}$ of the low-degree code (Definition~\ref{def:decoding-map}, applied with $H = \F_q$; see Remark~\ref{rem:qld-decoding-identity}), which maps a polynomial $g$ to the string of its evaluations on the hypercube $\{0,1\}^m$; and the low-degree encoding $h \mapsto g_h$ together with the vectors $\mathrm{ind}_m(u) \in \F_q^M$, characterized by $h \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u) = g_h(u)$ for all $u \in \F_q^m$ \eqref{eq:low-degree-encoding-definition}. Both maps are $\F_q$-linear, and $\mathrm{Dec}(g_h) = h$ for every $h \in \F_q^{M}$. We call a polynomial $g \in \mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$ an \emph{encoding} if $g = g_h$ for some $h \in \F_q^{M}$ or, equivalently, if $g$ is multilinear; since a multilinear polynomial is determined by its values on $\{0,1\}^m$, the encodings are exactly the $g$ with $g_{\mathrm{Dec}(g)} = g$ as polynomial representatives, and
 \[
 	\mathrm{Dec}(g) \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u) = g(u)
 	\qquad \text{for every encoding $g$ and every } u \in \F_q^m\;.
 \]
 For a $g$ that is not an encoding the two sides of this identity are the evaluations of the distinct polynomial representatives $g_{\mathrm{Dec}(g)}$ and $g$; when $d \leq q-1$ they consequently disagree at some $u$, but when $d \geq q$ the two representatives may induce the same function on $\F_q^m$, so pointwise validity of the identity does not characterize the encodings; see Remark~\ref{rem:qld-decoding-identity}.

 	The source states the constructions of this chapter in terms of its boolean decoding map (the case $H = \{0,1\}$ of Definition~\ref{def:decoding-map}) while describing that map as returning the string of \emph{all} evaluations of $g$ on the hypercube. The source further asserts the identity $\mathrm{Dec}(g) \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u) = g(u)$ for every $g \in \mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$. Since the left-hand side equals $g_{\mathrm{Dec}(g)}(u)$, the identity, taken for all $u \in \F_q^m$, states that the multilinear representative $g_{\mathrm{Dec}(g)}$ and $g$ induce the same function on $\F_q^m$.  \begin{lemma}[Preservation of the robustness error family]\label{lem:qld-extraction-error-form}
 	\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.deltaExtract_le_deltaQld}
 	\uses{def:admissible, lem:qld-unitary}
 	Let $C\geq1$, $a>1$, and $0<b<1$. Suppose that
 	\[
 		\delta_G=a(md)^a\bigl(\eps^b+q^{-b}+2^{-bmd}\bigr),
 		\qquad
 		\delta_P=C\left(\delta_G+\sqrt{\eps}+\frac{md}{q}\right),

 	$a'\geq1$ and $0<b'<1$, depending only on $C,a,b$, such that, for every
 	admissible $(q,m,d)$ and every $0\leq\eps\leq1$,
 	\[
 		\delta_{\mathrm{ext}}
 		\leq a'(md)^{a'}\bigl(\eps^{b'}+q^{-b'}+2^{-b'md}\bigr).

 \begin{remark}[Two steps in the source proof of the extraction lemma]\label{rem:qld-unitary-triangle-slip}
 	In the source proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-unitary}, the triangle inequality gives $\| H_X \ket{\vartheta} - H_Z \ket{\vartheta} \| \leq \| (\Id - H_X)\ket{\vartheta} \| + \| (\Id - H_Z)\ket{\vartheta} \| \leq 2\sqrt{\delta_P}$, so that $\| H_X \ket{\vartheta} - H_Z \ket{\vartheta} \|^2 \leq 4\delta_P$; the source instead asserts the bound $2\sqrt{\delta_P}$ for the \emph{squared} norm, which holds only when $\sqrt{\delta_P} \leq 1/2$, and consequently carries the term $\sqrt{\delta_P}$ into an overlap bound of $1 - 2\delta_P - \sqrt{\delta_P}$. The proof above uses the corrected bound $4\delta_P$, which gives the overlap bound $1 - 4\delta_P$ and leaves the final bound $\delta_{\mathrm{qld}} = O(\delta_P^{1/4} + md/q)$ unchanged. The source proof also normalizes the vector $(\bra{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M})_{\mathrm{A}''\mathrm{B}''} \ket{\vartheta}$ without ensuring that it is nonzero; the case distinction on $\delta_P$ in the proof above supplies this, the conclusions of the lemma being trivial when $\delta_P$ exceeds a universal constant.
 	The numerical corrections and their role in the extraction argument are
 	documented in \cite{gap:qpbt_extraction-transfer}.
 \end{remark}

 \section{The range-projection obligation}
 
 Lines~1827--1858 prove state-dependent closeness for the concrete operators
 obtained by conjugating the original measurement with the swap unitaries.
 Lines~1864--1875 then define isometries by adjoining EPR pairs and applying
 those unitaries, and immediately state the corresponding closeness for
 $\phi M_h\phi^\dagger$.  The omitted range projection makes this implication
 non-definitional \cite[lines~1827--1875]{Ji2020MIPStar}.
 
 Let $\Psi$ be the original state and suppose $\phi\Psi$ is close to the ideal
 state $\Delta$.  Since $Q\phi\Psi=\phi\Psi$ and $Q$ is a contraction, the
 triangle inequality bounds $(I-Q)\Delta$ by the state-extraction error.  Using
 $\phi M_h\phi^\dagger=N_hQ$, split
 \[
   (N_hQ-T_h)\Delta
   =(N_h-T_h)\Delta-N_h(I-Q)\Delta,
 \]
 where $T_h$ is the ideal Pauli projector.  Summing squared norms over $h$
 uses projectivity and orthogonality to keep the second term under control.
 The same argument is required for each player and each Pauli basis.
 
 This transfer is an open proof obligation for the next extraction stage.  It
 must be a theorem derived from the concrete swap unitaries, transformed-state
 estimate, and operator comparisons.  It must not be stored as a bridge field,
 residual assumption, or hypothesis of the source-labelled soundness theorem.
